Root (`/dev/md2`, 436G) hit 99% on 2026-09-16 and forced a reboot. `/data` (938G) had 729G free.
Root writers: Docker root at `/var/lib/docker` (~180G: two SeaweedFS volumes 90G, images, dev-stack layers),
14+ agenta checkouts under `~/code` (node_modules 51G), pnpm store 11G, opencode 22G, uv/playwright caches.

- `~/devbox-cleanup.sh` runs nightly at 04:30 (crontab). On 2026-09-16 I added `docker image prune -a`
  (7 days), uv/pnpm/playwright cache prune, and a disk warning. `~/memwatch.sh` (every 5 min) now
  `wall`s when / has under 10% free. Neither script ever stops a stack.
- `/etc/cron.d/agenta-oss-team-store-backup` (root, 03:30) rsyncs the `agenta-oss-team_seaweed-data`
  volume to `/data/backups/seaweedfs/oss-team` with 14-day retention. NEVER tear down or move the
  oss-team stack or that volume without Mahmoud. Moving the Docker root would change its SOURCE path.

Post-incident safety net for the `agenta-oss-team` SeaweedFS store while it had

**REMOVE AFTER:** once bucket versioning on oss-team has been verified for 30 days.

The docker volume `agenta-oss-team_seaweed-data`

crash-consistent copy taken while the container keeps running; it is not a
per-bucket or per-drive backup, it is the whole store.

Nightly at 03:30 local time via the root crontab entry in
`/etc/cron.d/agenta-oss-team-store-backup`, which runs
`/usr/local/sbin/agenta-oss-team-store-backup.sh`.

  are actually written to disk)
- logs to `/data/backups/seaweedfs/oss-team/backup.log`
- prunes snapshots older than 14 days

content.text:
I found why the oss-team backups are so large. No single stray file is the cause. A few agent chat sessions in the team's "Main Workspace" project kept their full conversation logs on the team drive, and those logs grew very large.

Each agent session gets its own working folder on the store. The coding tools write a log of every turn into that folder. Codex writes to `.codex/sessions`, and the other harnesses write to `agents/sessions`. Long sessions make these logs grow for weeks. The largest session folders are:

| Session folder (created) | Size | What fills it |
|---|---|---|
| `01a0a184…` (Sep 14) | 45.6 GB | 32 GB of Codex logs, 12 GB of agent session logs |
| `01a0a486…` (Sep 15) | 20.6 GB | Codex logs |
| `01a13f56…` (Oct 15) | 16.8 GB | Agent session logs |
| `01a0a419…` (Sep 15) | 10.3 GB | Codex logs |
| Two more (Sep 15, Sep 21) | 15.4 GB | Not broken down |

Together, these six sessions hold about 110 GB of the 131 GB store. The store has almost no data left over from deleted files (about 13 GB), so a compaction would free little.

You have two ways to make the backups smaller:

1. **Delete the old logs in those sessions.** This frees the most space, both in the store and in every backup. But it is the team's live data. The people who use those sessions would lose their history, and a session may stop resuming. I recommend that you or the team decide which sessions are finished. I will not delete anything there on my own.
2. **Keep fewer backups.** Today the script keeps the newest snapshot plus up to two weekly ones. Because the log files change every night, each snapshot is a full 110 to 130 GB copy (hard links save almost nothing). If the script keeps only the newest snapshot, it saves about 110 GB. The cost is that you can only restore last night's state.

With 352 GB free, nothing is urgent now. Tonight's backup will run again.

<result>## 1. Retention: is there any?

**Answer: No for the session itself, its turns, its mounts and the harness logs. Those are kept forever. Two narrow exceptions apply: session records (the event log) in EE cloud plans, and old object versions on the bundled SeaweedFS.**

**Nothing purges sessions, turns, interactions or mounts.**
- I found no TTL, retention setting or scheduled job for `session_streams`, `session_turns`, `session_interactions`, `session_inputs`, `session_commands` or `mounts`.
- Searching `api/oss/src/core/sessions`, `core/mounts`, `dbs/postgres/{sessions,mounts}`, `api/ee/src/core/sessions` and `api/entrypoints` for retention, TTL, purge, sweep, cleanup and prune finds no such job. There is also no query that deletes rows by `deleted_at` age anywhere in `api/oss/src` or `api/ee/src`.
- The OSS cron jobs are `api/oss/src/crons/{gateways,queries,triggers}.txt`. They only call the OAuth-attempt sweep, evaluation-run refresh and trigger-schedule refresh. None of them touches sessions or mounts.
- Archiving is soft and reversible. It sets `deleted_at` on the stream row and the session's mounts (`api/oss/src/core/sessions/service.py:369-400`, `api/oss/src/core/mounts/service.py:981-1029`). Nothing ever purges archived items later.
- Generic mounts can only be archived (`mounts/service.py:905`). Outside session delete, they have no hard-delete path.
- The startup "orphan sweep" (`api/entrypoints/routers.py:384-392`) only settles dead executions. It deletes nothing.

**Exception 1 (EE only): retention for session records.**
- Session records are the `records` table, which is the session event log.
- Cron: `api/ee/src/crons/records.txt` runs at minutes 14 and 44 of every hour. It calls `POST /admin/records/flush` (`api/ee/src/crons/records.sh`, router at `api/ee/src/apis/fastapi/sessions/records/router.py:1-60`, mounted at `api/ee/src/main.py:169`).
- `RecordsRetentionService.flush_records` deletes rows whose `created_at` is older than the cutoff, plan by plan (`api/ee/src/core/sessions/records/service.py:26-122`, `api/ee/src/dbs/postgres/sessions/records/dao.py` around lines 89-121).
- The retention period comes from the plan's `Counter.RECORDS_INGESTED` setting in `api/ee/src/core/access/entitlements/types.py`:
  - Hobby: weekly, 7 days (line 358-359)
  - Pro: monthly, 31 days (line 450-451)
  - Business: quarterly, 92 days (line 540-541)
  - `CLOUD_V0_AGENTA_AI` (line 627) and `SELF_HOSTED_ENTERPRISE` (line 665): no retention set, so records are skipped ("unlimited retention").
- OSS has no records retention at all.
- This only deletes records. Turns, streams and mounts stay. `service.py:6` and `:350` say that tracing retention owns records.

**Harness logs (`.codex/sessions`, `agents/sessions`): kept forever.**
- The runner deliberately writes them to the durable cwd mount so that native resume survives a sandbox replacement (`services/runner/src/engines/sandbox_agent/codex-assets.ts:1-5`, `:41-45`; Pi works the same way at `pi-assets.ts:872`, `:882`).
- The runner's `rmSync` calls only clear local sandbox directories (`session-pool.ts:156`, `:325`, `pi-assets.ts:851`). They never touch object storage.
- These files are removed only when the session is hard-deleted (section 2).

**`.versions` and old object versions.**
- The `.versions` folders are not created by Agenta code. Searching for `.versions` finds nothing related. They are most likely how SeaweedFS stores object versions internally, which follows from bucket versioning being on.
- `store.ensure_version_retention` (`api/oss/src/core/store/storage.py:203-247`) runs at API startup (`api/entrypoints/routers.py:367-382`). It does two things:
  - turns on bucket versioning;
  - installs a lifecycle rule named `agenta-noncurrent-version-expiration` with `NoncurrentVersionExpiration(noncurrent_days=N)` on the whole bucket (prefix `""`) (`storage.py:40`, `:268-290`).
- `N` is `AGENTA_STORE_VERSION_RETENTION_DAYS`, which defaults to 30 (`api/oss/src/utils/env.py:1580-1588`, `:1626-1632`).
- Setting `N` to 0 removes the rule but leaves versioning on (`storage.py:225-234`). Old versions would then be kept forever. The docs at `docs/docs/self-host/agents/06-back-up-agent-files.mdx` say 0 "turns the whole thing off", which does not match the code.
- This applies to the bundled SeaweedFS only (`storage.py:220`, `is_seaweedfs` at `:164-168`). For a remote S3 bucket, versioning and lifecycle are left to the operator.
- Only noncurrent versions expire. Current files are never expired.
- One thing I could not confirm: whether SeaweedFS 4.47, started as plain `weed server ... -s3` (`hosting/kubernetes/helm/templates/seaweedfs-statefulset.yaml:66`), actually enforces `NoncurrentVersionExpiration`. Nothing in the repo checks this.

## 2. Deletion

There are three different "delete" operations.

| Operation | Endpoint | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Delete session | **`DELETE /sessions/?session_id=<id>`** (operation `delete_session`, permission `EDIT_SESSIONS`) | **Hard delete, including the mount storage** |
| Archive session | `POST /sessions/archive`, reversed by `POST /sessions/unarchive` | Soft (`deleted_at`) on the stream row and the mounts. Files are untouched |
| Kill session | `DELETE /sessions/streams/?session_id=<id>` (operation `delete_session_stream`, permission `RUN_SESSIONS`) | Tears down the sandbox, cancels pending interactions, and soft-deletes the stream row. Mounts and files are untouched |

The delete and archive routes are at `api/oss/src/apis/fastapi/sessions/router.py:2117-2160`, and the delete handler is at `:2408-2430`. The kill route is at `router.py:445-450`, its handler at `:630-660`, and the soft delete at `streams/service.py:415-430`.

**What hard delete does.** `SessionsService.delete_session` (`api/oss/src/core/sessions/service.py:336-367`) runs these steps:
1. Hard-deletes `session_turns` (`turns/dao.py:331-339`, `sa_delete`).
2. Hard-deletes `session_interactions` (`interactions/dao.py:281-290`).
3. Calls `mounts_service.delete_session_mounts` (`api/oss/src/core/mounts/service.py:958-979`). This:
   - hard-deletes every mount row with that `session_id` (`dbs/postgres/mounts/dao.py:237-262`);
   - then calls `delete_prefix` on `[<namespace>/]mounts/<project_id>/<mount_id>/` for each mount (prefix built at `service.py:447-460`).
   - This covers the `__ag__session__<uuid5>__cwd` mount, including `.codex/sessions` and `agents/sessions`, and the attachments mount.
4. Hard-deletes the stream row (`streams/service.py:1134-1149`).

**What hard delete leaves behind.**
- Records are deliberately kept (`service.py:350`).
- `session_inputs`, `session_commands`, `session_executions` and `session_attachments` rows are not touched by this fan-out.

**Caveats on purging the files.**
- `delete_prefix` (`api/oss/src/core/store/storage.py:742-751`) lists the current keys and calls `remove_objects` without version IDs (`delete_keys` at `:723-740`). On the versioned bundled SeaweedFS, this only writes delete markers. The file contents stay as noncurrent versions until the 30-day lifecycle rule expires them, and only if SeaweedFS enforces that rule.
- On a remote S3 bucket where the operator turned versioning on, the contents stay until the operator's own lifecycle policy removes them.
- So the files are not purged immediately.
- Storage deletion is skipped silently if `mounts_store` or `bucket` is not configured (`mounts/service.py:972`).

**Admin path.** There is no admin endpoint that hard-deletes a session or purges mount storage. The only `/admin` routes are billing, spans, events, records, triggers, gateways, evaluations and accounts (`api/ee/src/main.py:148-169`, `api/entrypoints/routers.py:1988`, `:2025`, `:2039`, `:2115`).
- `delete_prefix` has exactly one caller, `delete_session_mounts`.
- Deleting a project cascades the `mounts` rows through a foreign key (`dbs/postgres/mounts/dbes.py:17-21`). It does not delete the objects under `mounts/<project_id>/`, so those are left orphaned.

**Bottom line:**
- **Kept forever?** Yes: session rows, turns, harness logs and cwd mount files stay until the user deletes the session. Archiving and killing do not remove them.
- **Exceptions:** EE cloud plans prune records after 7, 31 or 92 days. The bundled SeaweedFS expires noncurrent object versions after 30 days by default.
- **Hard delete with storage:** `DELETE /sessions/?session_id=` is the only path. It removes the rows and the current objects, but on versioned storage the old versions remain until the lifecycle rule expires them.</result>

        action: Action,
        project_id: UUID,

        if not isinstance(action, Permission) or action not in (
            _SESSION_READ_ACTIONS | {Permission.RUN_SESSIONS, Permission.EDIT_SESSIONS}

        # The read assigns a legacy row its owner first, whatever the action.
        access, tombstone = await self._session_access_or_tombstone(
            project_id=project_id, session_id=session_id
        )
        if access is None and tombstone is not None:
            # A deleted private session: its records stay with tracing retention. Its
            # former owner may still read them; nobody may write to the id again (no
            # session is created over a tombstone), and everyone else is answered as
            # for a hidden session.
            if action in _SESSION_READ_ACTIONS and _is_human(
                principal, tombstone.owner_user_id
            ):
                return None
            return DecisionReason.RESOURCE_DENIED
        if access is None:
            _note_missing_session(project_id=project_id, session_id=session_id)
            return None  # no such session

        policy = access.policy
        owner = policy.owner_user_id
        if (
            access.is_channel

            and principal.kind == PrincipalKind.INSTALLATION
            and _binding_creator(principal) == owner

            # the owner's own channel bindings read, run and edit it. (A project-visible
            # channel session is ownerless: S1, S2 and S4 let any binding act there.)
            return None

The six sessions are deleted. A background job now waits for SeaweedFS to finish freeing the chunks and then compacts the store. I will report the final sizes when it ends.

**Answer to your retention question: yes, chats are kept forever.** Here is what the code does today:

- **Sessions, turns, and drive files have no retention rule.** No cron job or worker removes them. Archiving a chat only hides it, and you can undo it. Only a hard delete (`DELETE /sessions/?session_id=`) removes the data.
- **The harness logs grow without a limit.** The runner writes the Codex and Pi conversation logs into the session's drive folder on purpose, so a session can resume after its sandbox is replaced (`services/runner/src/engines/sandbox_agent/codex-assets.ts`). Nothing ever trims them. That is how one session reached 45 GB.
- **Delete does not really free storage on our bundled SeaweedFS.** The bucket has versioning turned on, so a delete only adds a "deleted" marker. The data stays as an old version. The API installs a rule that expires old versions after 30 days (`AGENTA_STORE_VERSION_RETENTION_DAYS`, `api/oss/src/core/store/storage.py:203`). But the old files of these sessions were still there, so I am not sure that SeaweedFS 4.47 applies the rule. That is why I removed the six folders directly in the store.
- **Only EE cloud has one retention rule, and it is narrow.** It deletes the session event records after 7, 31 or 92 days, based on the plan (`api/ee/src/core/sessions/records/service.py`). It does not touch turns, sessions, or drive files.

Two smaller problems turned up:
- Only the human owner can delete a session that has an owner. An API key cannot do it, even the owner's own key. To delete your five sessions, I had to call the API's delete code directly inside the container.
- Deleting a project removes its mount rows but leaves its files in the store forever.

I will send the final store size and free disk space when the compaction finishes.

# Write Issues

Write issues a teammate can act on without asking you follow-up questions. Lead with what
the reader needs to reproduce or understand the request, not with your analysis.

Show a draft first and let the user react before you create anything in Linear.

## 1. Title

Prefix the title with the type in parentheses, the same way the repo prefixes PRs.

- `(bug)` for something broken.
- `(feat)` for a new capability or improvement.
- Other types as needed: `(chore)`, `(docs)`.

State the symptom or the request in plain words. Keep it short.

- Good: `(bug) Feedback sent via the API can't be filtered in observability`
- Good: `(feat) Filter evaluation results by metric value`
- Bad: `(bug) Annotation filter options array empty due to thin refs` (that is the root cause, not the symptom)
- Bad: `Observability issue` (vague)

## 2. Body — bugs

Do not open with a "Context" heading. Start with the reproduction, in the user's voice:
when I do this, I expect that, but instead this happens. Or: this code is supposed to do
X, but it does Y. Keep the words simple.

Then give the concrete information a teammate needs to debug it, when you have it:

- Exact steps to reproduce, numbered.
- Requests and responses (the call you made and what came back).
- Errors, console output, or relevant log lines.
- Screenshots or screen recordings.
- Where it reproduces (local, preview, Railway, cloud) and the version if known.

That is the whole job: make it reproducible. Include real payloads over descriptions of
them.

## 3. Do not write the root cause

The issue tracks the problem, not the investigation. Do not add a "root cause" or "why
this happens" section. That analysis belongs in the PR that fixes it (see the
`write-pr-description` skill). Keep the issue about observable behavior and the
information needed to debug it.

If you already know the cause, it still does not go in the issue body. Put it in the PR.

## 4. Body — feature requests

Lead with the problem or the goal from the user's point of view: what they are trying to
do and why it is hard today. Then describe the behavior they want. Skip implementation
design unless the user asked for it.

## 5. Todo list

Add a checkbox list only when delivery is split across stacked PRs or has several ordered
steps. One line per step, written as an outcome.

```
- [ ] Fix the filter so it reads the evaluator's real feedback metrics.
- [ ] Fix how the frontend reads the feedback type so the nested schema is understood.
```

If a single PR closes the whole issue, skip the todo list. Do not pad an issue with
checkboxes for its own sake.

File issues on the **Agenta** team (key `AGE`). Pick the fields deliberately.

input.content:
When people use agent chats for a few weeks, the object store grows without a limit, and deleting chats does not give the space back. On a self-hosted deployment with the bundled SeaweedFS, six long chat sessions held about 110 GB of the 131 GB store. Most of it was harness conversation logs (`.codex/sessions` and `agents/sessions`) inside each session's working-directory mount. One session alone held 45 GB.

I expect old chats to expire under some retention rule, and I expect a deleted chat to free its storage. Instead, four things happen:

1. **Nothing ever expires chats.** Session rows, turns, and the session's mount files (including the harness logs) stay until someone deletes the session by hand. Archiving only hides the session. No cron job or worker removes old sessions or trims harness logs. (EE plans expire session records after 7, 31 or 92 days, but turns, sessions and mount files stay.)
2. **Deleting a session does not free storage on the bundled SeaweedFS.** `DELETE /sessions/?session_id=<id>` removes the database rows and the current objects. Because the bucket has versioning turned on, the files stay as noncurrent versions. After the delete, `fs.du` on the mount prefix showed the same size as before (45.6 GB). The space came back only after removing the prefix with `weed shell fs.rm -r` and running `volume.vacuum`. The 30-day noncurrent-version rule (`AGENTA_STORE_VERSION_RETENTION_DAYS`) should cover this, but it is not clear that SeaweedFS 4.47 applies it.
3. **An API key cannot delete an owned session, even the owner's own key.** `DELETE /sessions/?session_id=<id>` with `Authorization: ApiKey <key of the session owner>` returns:
   ```json
   {"detail":{"code":"access_denied","message":"Access denied: the run's principal cannot do this in the project.","details":{"reason":"resource_denied","principal_kind":"api_key"}}}
   ```
   The same call works for a session without an owner. So an operator cannot clean up storage through the API. The only way is the UI, one session at a time, signed in as each owner.
4. **Deleting a project leaves its mount files in the store.** The `mounts` rows go away with the project, but nothing deletes the objects under `mounts/<project_id>/`. They stay in the store with nothing pointing to them.

## Steps to reproduce (item 2)

1. Run a self-hosted stack with the bundled SeaweedFS (version 4.47).
2. Start an agent chat and run a few turns, so the session cwd mount has files.
3. Delete the session: `DELETE /api/sessions/?session_id=<id>` as the owner (from the UI).
4. In the SeaweedFS container, run `echo "fs.du /buckets/agenta-store/mounts/<project_id>/<mount_id>" | weed shell`. The size is unchanged, and the folder contains only `*.versions` entries.

Seen on v0.125.2, docker-compose OSS.

## Todo

- [ ] Add a retention setting for agent chats (sessions, turns and session mount files) and a job that applies it.
- [ ] Make a session delete free its storage on versioned buckets (remove the object versions, not only add delete markers), and confirm the noncurrent-version rule really runs on the bundled SeaweedFS.
- [ ] Give operators a way to delete sessions through the API (for example, a project admin or an admin endpoint).
- [ ] Delete a project's mount objects when the project is deleted.
